stories.headline: Flood scare in MP: IAF helicopters, SDRF teams deployed as Mandakini river overflows
stories.title: Flood scare in MP: IAF helicopters, SDRF teams deployed as Mandakini river overflows
stories.summary: Indian Air Force helicopters were deployed to rescue stranded people in Chitrakoot. Torrential rains caused the Mandakini river to overflow, flooding large parts of the town. Three State Disaster Response Force teams were also engaged in shifting people to safer places. A dam breach in Uttar Pradesh worsened the situation, while relief shelters were prepared. The water level in the Mandakini had started receding Saturday night after rainfall paused.

stories.headline: Nepal seeks to import power earlier from India after flood devastation, asks for approvals
stories.title: Nepal seeks to import power earlier from India after flood devastation, asks for approvals
stories.summary: While the Himalayan country usually imports electricity from India during the winter months, it has now asked that the required approvals for sending power be processed in September itself
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: In the wake of the devastating flash flood that severely impacted Nepal’s power infrastructure, Kathmandu has asked India to give the requisite approvals for the transmission of electricity to Nepal earlier than usual, senior officials in the Union Power Ministry said on Saturday (August 29, 2026).
“Nepal has asked that India advance import approvals, starting from September this year, in view of the generation deficits caused by this disaster.
The concerned authorities are processing the requests,” an official said.
According to officials, India is willing to provide any additional power that Nepal may need.
Nepal usually imports electricity from India during the winter months, starting around October, as power generation is typically low in the Himalayan country during the freezing winter months.
Conversely, the country exports its excess hydropower to India during the summer.
According to official data, India imported 3,299 million units (MUs) of power from Nepal in fiscal year 2025-26 and exported 1,451 MUs to it.
Transmission of electricity across India’s borders requires mandatory clearances from the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), among others.
According to an internal assessment, Nepal’s electricity generation capacity has declined by about 550 megawatts because of the infrastructural damage induced by the flood.
Officials said that this resulted in the cross-border power flow to India reducing by approximately 400 MW from earlier peaks of 950 MW to 1,000 MW.
However, the officials assured that India was not foreseeing any requirement to make alternative arrangements to compensate for the shortfall.

“We do not foresee any requirement for exceptional emergency procurement or alternative arrangement to balance domestic demand,” an official said, adding, “India’s vast national grid capacity and robust generation reserve margins are capable of absorbing a temporary shortfall of 400 MW seamlessly without disrupting grid stability or retail supply."

stories.headline: Tharoor urges Centre to deploy full NDRF contingent for Nepal flood rescue
stories.title: Tharoor urges Centre to deploy full NDRF contingent for Nepal flood rescue
stories.summary: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor urged the Centre to deploy a full NDRF contingent, heavy-lift helicopters and advanced search equipment in Nepal, where hundreds of Indians remain missing or stranded after devastating flash floods, stressing that rescue efforts must be intensified immediately
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: New Delhi: With several Indians still missing in the Nepal flash floods, Congress MP Shashi Tharoor on Saturday asked the Modi government for a full NDRF contingent and heavy-lift helicopters for rescue operations.
In his letter to External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, Tharoor urged the government to pull out all stops to rescue the stranded or those who may still be alive beneath the debris.

On Wednesday, an ice-rock avalanche following a glacial collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border sent a torrent of water, mud and debris downstream, wiping out towns and villages, damaging crucial infrastructure and washing away hydropower stations through central Nepal.
“Every hour that passes narrows the ground on which hope can still stand,” the MP from Thiruvananthapuram said.
“I am writing to you regarding the Indian nationals who remain missing following the flash floods that struck Nepal on 26 August.
India’s response has been swift and substantial.

The Prime Minister’s early outreach to Kathmandu, the four tranches of relief material, the eleven-member team of doctors, paramedics and tunnel rescue experts, and the control room and Embassy helplines have all made a difference,” Tharoor said.
India’s Ambassador to Nepal Naveem Srivastava and his team have worked round-the-clock, he noted.
“The return of the group from Tibet, whom you personally received at the airport, gave many families their first moment of hope in three days.
The rescue of the Indian workers at Trishuli- 1 was a genuine triumph,” he said.
“Families have noticed all of this.
Several have asked me to convey their gratitude to you personally, and I am glad to do so.

stories.headline: Civic agencies to strengthen flood preparedness at vulnerable locations in Chennai
stories.title: Civic agencies to strengthen flood preparedness at vulnerable locations in Chennai
stories.summary: Out of 207 identified vulnerable locations in GCC, stormwater drains have been constructed in 117 locations
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Civic agencies have started identifying vulnerable locations that are prone to flooding owing to large infrastructure projects including Metrorail, Tangedco and Metrowater in the city.
Owing to intensifying El Niño, Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay has ordered an allocation of ₹100 crore to execute comprehensive precautionary measures against Northeast Monsoon.
Civic agencies will also implement an action plan for vulnerable locations and provide alternate solutions to prevent flooding this monsoon.

MAWS secretary Gagandeep Singh Bedi conducted a meeting in Ripon Buildings on Saturday with officials of various civic agencies to strengthen monsoon preparedness activities in the city, in the presence of CMRL Managing Director Ashish Chatterjee and Greater Chennai Corporation Commissioner G.S. Sameeran, and senior officials from key stakeholder departments, including WRD, Highways, NHAI, Tangedco, Metrowater, Southern Railway and others.

Out of 207 identified vulnerable locations inside GCC limits, stormwater drains have been constructed in 117 locations, modular storage tanks with high-capacity discharge pumps have been installed in 20 locations, dedicated motor pumps are stationed at 48 locations, and alternate engineering solutions will be implemented for the remaining areas.

The funding of ₹100 crore covers stormwater drain desilting and ward-level relief preparedness, road restoration and repair, procurement and maintenance of heavy-duty motor pumps and deployment of 1,000 seasonal workers for monsoon related works.
A total of 36 GCC boats and 275 fishing boats, arranged via the Fisheries Department, along with trained operators, will be kept on standby.
A total of 215 flood relief centres and 111 community kitchens will be readied.
Desilting is actively under way across 1,671 km of stormwater drains and 1,10,082 silt catch pits throughout the city.
Heavy machinery, motor pumps, and mechanised tree-cutters have been placed on standby.
Over 1,000 general volunteers and 721.
Residents Welfare Association members have been mobilised.

stories.headline: India ready to provide all possible assistance: Rajnath Singh on flash floods in Nepal
stories.title: India ready to provide all possible assistance: Rajnath Singh on flash floods in Nepal
stories.summary: Lucknow , August 29: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Saturday said India was deeply concerned over the devastating flash floods in Nepal and was ready to provide all possible assistance to the neighbouring country. Speaking to reporters in Lucknow, Singh said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had made it clear that India would provide whatever assistance Nepal requires and added that relief support was being sent continuously. "The crisis situation in Nepal is not only worrying the people of Nepal, but India is also concerned about it. The Prime Minister has very clearly stated that whatever assistance is needed, India is ready to provide all of it, and we have started sending assistance continuously," Singh said. According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), the death toll in the Bhote Koshi flood-related disaster in Nepal has reached 626, while 2,426 people are still missing. As per the latest search, rescue and relief update issued by the NDRRMA at 10 am on August 29, Chitwan reported the highest number of deaths, with 233 bodies, including human remains, recovered from the area. Nawalparasi East reported 158 deaths, followed by Nuwakot with 51, Gorkha with 48, Nawalparasi West with 47, Dhading with 45, Tanahun with 31 and Rasua with 13. Other affected areas also reported deaths. The authority said that 2,426 people remained missing. The list includes 27 Nepal Police personnel, 45 Nepal Army personnel, 13 Armed Police Force personnel, 15 Customs Office personnel and four Immigration Office personnel. India has been coordinating relief and rescue efforts in response to the disaster in Nepal, while authorities continue to monitor the situation and the condition of Indian nationals affected by the floods. Nepal President Ramchandra Paudel also expressed gratitude towards India for support and solidarity following a devastating flash flood. Paudel also condoled the demise of Indian nationals in Nepal. (ANI)

stories.headline: Power Tariff Hike: Omar Government Adds to the Burden of the People of Jammu & Kashmir
stories.title: Power Tariff Hike: Omar Government Adds to the Burden of the People of Jammu & Kashmir
stories.summary: ADV SUNIL SETHI The decision to increase electricity tariffs in Jammu & Kashmir at a time when ordinary families are already struggling with the rising cost of living is deeply disappointing. More importantly, it raises a fundamental question of political accountability: what happened to the promises made to the people before the Assembly elections? The Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission has approved an average tariff increase of 6.83 per cent, applicable from September 1, 2026. For metered domestic consumers, the rate for consumption up to 200 units has increased from ₹2.30 to ₹2.45 per unit; for 201–400 units, from ₹4.00 to ₹4.20; and above 400 units, from ₹4.35 to ₹4.60 per unit. These figures may appear small when viewed from the comfort of government offices. For an ordinary household, however, every additional financial burden matters. From Promise of Relief to Reality of Higher Bills The National Conference went before the electorate promising 200 units of free electricity. That promise naturally created expectations among families that desperately needed relief. Today, instead of experiencing the promised relief, consumers are confronting increased tariffs. The government may argue that its promise of free electricity and the general electricity tariff are technically separate matters. But politics cannot be reduced to technical explanations. The real question is what an ordinary voter understood when promises of cheaper or free electricity were made. People vote on the basis of promises and the reasonable expectations created by those promises. If financial constraints, distribution losses and the cost of purchasing electricity were realities after the election, they were realities before the election as well. Governments cannot discover economic realities only after obtaining the mandate of the people. Kashmir's Winter Cannot Be Viewed Through Ordinary Consumption Calculations The impact of electricity prices assumes an even greater significance in the Kashmir Valley. For people sitting outside Kashmir, electricity may be regarded primarily as a source of lighting and running household appliances. During Kashmir's severe winter, electricity is intimately connected with survival, warmth and basic human comfort. Temperatures fall below freezing in many areas. Water pipes freeze. Snowfall disrupts normal life. Families depend increasingly upon electric heaters, boilers, geysers, heating blankets and other appliances. The elderly, children and economically weaker families suffer the most. This means that electricity consumption during the harsh winter months cannot simply be treated as discretionary consumption. A Kashmiri family using additional electricity to keep its children or elderly parents warm is not indulging in luxury. It is responding to climatic necessity. And the timing is particularly unfortunate. The revised tariff becomes applicable from September 1 and will remain applicable through the approaching winter until March 31, 2027. The government should therefore ask itself a simple question: Is the period immediately preceding the harsh Kashmir winter the appropriate time to make electricity more expensive for households? Don't Make Consumers Pay for Inefficiency There is undoubtedly a financial problem in the electricity sector. Power has a cost. Distribution companies require revenue, and transmission and distribution losses have historically presented a serious challenge. But the solution cannot perpetually be to transfer the consequences of inefficiency onto honest consumers. The first responsibility of government should be to reduce losses, improve billing and collection, prevent electricity theft, modernise infrastructure and improve the efficiency of distribution companies. A family that pays its electricity bill regularly should not become the easiest source for balancing the books. Before asking consumers to pay more, the government must demonstrate what measurable reduction it has achieved in distribution losses and what administrative reforms it has undertaken to bring down costs. Efficiency must come before additional burden. The Government's Defence Does Not Answer the Political Question Chief Minister Omar Abdullah has defended the increase by arguing that the government never promised that electricity tariffs would remain static and that power continues to be substantially subsidised. That may constitute an administrative defence. It does not answer the political question. The issue is not whether electricity continues to receive subsidy. The issue is whether the government is moving towards the relief that was promised to the electorate or away from it. The people were promised 200 units of free electricity. They are entitled to ask when that promise will translate into meaningful relief in their monthly household budgets. A government cannot seek political credit for promises and subsequently seek refuge behind regulatory calculations when people demand their implementation. BJP Must Stand With the Consumer The Bharatiya Janata Party should unequivocally stand with the ordinary electricity consumer of Jammu & Kashmir. This is not an issue concerning Jammu or Kashmir alone. A shopkeeper in Jammu, a middle-class employee in Kathua, a farmer in the countryside, a pensioner in Srinagar and a family facing the freezing winter in north or south Kashmir all ultimately confront the same question: How much more can the household budget absorb? The BJP should demand that the Omar Abdullah government reconsider the tariff increase, particularly its impact upon domestic consumers, and immediately place before the people a transparent roadmap for fulfilling its electricity-related electoral commitments. Special consideration should also be given to the extraordinary electricity requirements of Kashmir during the winter months. If necessary, the government should explore a targeted winter electricity relief mechanism for vulnerable and middle-income domestic consumers in the Valley rather than allowing climatic necessity to translate into financial punishment. Promises Carry a Moral Obligation Democracy does not end when votes are counted. An electoral promise creates a political and moral obligation. Governments must either implement their promises or candidly explain why they cannot do so. What they cannot reasonably do is promise relief while seeking votes and subsequently impose additional burdens after coming to power. The people of Jammu & Kashmir have endured decades of difficulties. They deserve governance that reduces their burdens rather than adding to them. The BJP must therefore raise its voice firmly, both inside and outside the Legislature, and demand: Withdraw or substantially reconsider the burden of the power tariff hike on domestic consumers. Protect Kashmir's households during the harsh winter. Reduce distribution losses before passing costs to consumers. And, above all, honour the commitments made to the people. Electricity in Jammu & Kashmir—particularly during a Kashmir winter—is not merely another commodity. For many families, it is warmth. It is security. It is a basic necessity of life. And a government elected on promises of relief should remember that before making that necessity more expensive. (The Author is the Chief Spokesperson of JK BJP)

The BJP should demand that the Omar Abdullah government reconsider the tariff increase, particularly its impact upon domestic consumers, and immediately place before the people a transparent roadmap for fulfilling its electricity-related electoral commitments.
Special consideration should also be given to the extraordinary electricity requirements of Kashmir during the winter months.

If necessary, the government should explore a targeted winter electricity relief mechanism for vulnerable and middle-income domestic consumers in the Valley rather than allowing climatic necessity to translate into financial punishment.
Promises Carry a Moral Obligation Democracy does not end when votes are counted.
An electoral promise creates a political and moral obligation.
Governments must either implement their promises or candidly explain why they cannot do so.
What they cannot reasonably do is promise relief while seeking votes and subsequently impose additional burdens after coming to power.
The people of Jammu & Kashmir have endured decades of difficulties.
They deserve governance that reduces their burdens rather than adding to them.
The BJP must therefore raise its voice firmly, both inside and outside the Legislature, and demand: Withdraw or substantially reconsider the burden of the power tariff hike on domestic consumers.
Protect Kashmir's households during the harsh winter.
Reduce distribution losses before passing costs to consumers.
And, above all, honour the commitments made to the people.
Electricity in Jammu & Kashmir—particularly during a Kashmir winter—is not merely another commodity.
For many families, it is warmth.
It is security.
It is a basic necessity of life.
And a government elected on promises of relief should remember that before making that necessity more expensive.
(The Author is the Chief Spokesperson of JK BJP).
